summary: Discovery + POC scoping focused on unit economics for a pilot using Redwood inference. transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, does the time still work?
[00:05] Karen Patel: Yes all good, thanks Maya.
[00:09] Liam Ortiz: Hi all, Liam from Redwood, SE on the call.
[00:12] Sofia Martinez: Hi, Sofia here. We're excited to talk through costs and the pilot.
[00:17] Maya Chen: Cool. Quick agenda: understand your workload, get the success criteria for the POC, go over cost modeling assumptions (per-token estimates), batching and cache knobs, and align on benchmark timeline.
[00:27] Jamal Rivers: Sounds good. For context, we currently run a hybrid inference pipeline, some on prem GPUs and some cloud endpoints. We want predictable cost and want to see if Redwood dedicated or hosted makes sense.
[00:36] Liam Ortiz: Got it. Can you share rough qps and token sizes? Even ballpark helps.
[00:41] Karen Patel: Sure. Typical online queries are 12 to 48 tokens in prompt, responses vary 40 to 150 tokens. Average conversation session about 300 tokens. Peak qps is about 120 requests/sec across a pool.
[00:50] Maya Chen: Nice that's helpful. So to map to unit economics we'll need average tokens per request, tokens per second at peak, and desired latency SLOs. What SLOs are you targeting?
[00:58] Sofia Martinez: We need p95 < 350ms for the majority of our user flows, and anything above 800ms needs a fallback. Cost target is under $X per active user monthly but that's high-level. For pilot we have a budget cap of $15k for the month of the test.
[01:12] Liam Ortiz: Understood. For p95 350ms with peak qps 120, we need to consider batching tradeoffs. Batching reduces per-token cost but increases latency due to queueing. We usually model the cost per 1M tokens with and without batching.
[01:25] Karen Patel: Can you talk through the per-token assumptions? We saw a quick number in the deck but want the granular calc.
[01:31] Maya Chen: Sure. Roughly, cost per token depends on model size, hardware, utilization, and quantization. For a hosted inference baseline on A100-equivalent, we model raw infra + amortized model + overhead. Example: baseline 1M tokens at 1.2x the model compute yields $Y, but with batching (batch size 8-16) and KV cache hit rates of 20-40% you can see 30-60% cost reductions.
[01:49] Liam Ortiz: To be more concrete, if your average sequence length per request is 250 tokens and batch size is 8, effective tokens/sec processed per GPU goes up, meaning fewer GPUs for same throughput. But if your latency window is tight, we might not be able to batch aggressively. So we produce two scenarios: (1) low-latency (minimal batching, conservative cache), (2) cost-optimized (larger batching, higher cache reliance, quantized weights).
[02:10] Jamal Rivers: What's the KV cache hit rate thing? We call some of our traffic repetitive prompts.
[02:15] Liam Ortiz: KV cache is prefix caching, so repeated system prompts or user history that's identical can be cached to avoid recomputing the early layers. If you have many repeated prefixes, hit rates can be significant. We ask you to provide workload traces so we can estimate realistic hit rates.
[02:27] Karen Patel: We'll share traces. One note: we have PII in some prompts so we need private deployment options or at minimum VPC peering and KMS.
[02:34] Maya Chen: Absolutely, Redwood Private or Dedicated with customer-managed KMS is an option. For the POC we can run in a dedicated sandbox with network controls. Jira to attach SOC2 docs, yeah.
[02:44] Sofia Martinez: Re: quantization and perf, how much quality regression do you expect if we quantize to 4-bit for the smaller models?
[02:51] Liam Ortiz: It depends on model family; often 4-bit QC gives 2-3% drop in certain benchmarks, sometimes negligible for retrieval-augmented flows. We'll include A/B quality checks in the benchmark plan.
[02:59] Maya Chen: Let's talk benchmarks. We propose running: 1) throughput sweep to find GPUs required at your QPS, 2) latency p50/p95 curves across concurrency and batch sizes, 3) cost per 1M tokens computation across the knobs (batch size, kv cache, quantization). We'll use your prompt set and a small synthetic heavy tail to model tail cases.
[03:20] Karen Patel: Timeline? We want results this week ideally.
[03:24] Liam Ortiz: We can run the baseline tests if we get traces and the prompt set by Monday. Benchmarks take 1-2 days to run and then a day to analyze. So earliest deliverable Friday if we start Monday.
[03:34] Jamal Rivers: There's an important network constraint: our VPC peering has a 10Gb cap and we have bursts. Is egress charged in your hosted?
[03:41] Maya Chen: In hosted it's counted as standard cloud egress. For the dedicated/private options we can profile and if bandwidth is an issue recommend a private deployment to avoid cloud egress and meet compliance.
[03:49] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[03:51] Liam Ortiz: Another callout: batching scheduler. Redwood supports dynamic batching with latency-aware thresholds; it will hold requests up to X ms or until batch size N is reached. For pilot we can tune that threshold.
[04:04] Karen Patel: Can you show a sample per-token math?
[04:07] Maya Chen: Quick example, just to illustrate. Assume model costs $C per GPU-hour (including infra), and 1 GPU-hour handles T tokens at your config. Then cost per token = C / T. Add a platform fee and monitoring overhead. So for 1M tokens if C/T = $0.20 per 1k tokens you get $200 per 1M tokens, then apply savings from caching/batching. (numbers illustrative).
[04:28] Jamal Rivers: Do you include developer operations costs in the model? We're trying to compare to our in-house infra.
[04:33] Liam Ortiz: We present two lanes: pure infra OPEX and full managed (includes SRE/monitoring/SLAs). The latter is higher but you'd save on staffing and faster time to operate. We'll include a sensitivity table in the spreadsheet.
[04:45] Sofia Martinez: For the POC success criteria Sofia: (laugh) sorry, Sofia speaking, ok success criteria from our side are: p95 < 350ms for 90% of flows, cost per active user month under your pilot target, accuracy/QA regression < 2% on our eval set. Also must pass security checklist.
[05:02] Maya Chen: Great. We'll make those explicit in the pilot plan as gating metrics.
[05:06] Karen Patel: One more: can you quantify the expected savings from prefix caching?
[05:10] Liam Ortiz: We'll estimate that once we ingest the traces. If 30% of tokens are repeated prefixes across sessions, you can see near proportional compute reduction on those prefixes. In some customers we've seen up to 40% effective compute reduction on RL prompt-heavy flows. But it depends.
[05:25] Maya Chen: Ok let's talk specifics for the run: what model families are you evaluating?
[05:29] Karen Patel: We're testing a 7B open LM and a 13B variant for quality. Also want to evaluate a quantized 30B variant if the perf is competitive.
[05:38] Liam Ortiz: Perfect. We'll run 7B and 13B baselines and a quantized 30B to compare quality/cost. For each we'll measure p50/p95, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens with batching levels 1, 4, 8, 16.
[05:51] Jamal Rivers: If you run the cost calc can you also model committed capacity discounts? We might be open to a 3 month commit if it lowers unit costs.
[05:58] Maya Chen: Yes we can model committed vs on-demand. We'll include a curve of price vs commitment level in the spreadsheet.
[06:05] Sofia Martinez: How do you handle unpredictable spikes? We need graceful degradation.
[06:10] Liam Ortiz: Redwood routing supports fallback to a smaller model, region failover, or rate-limited degradation. We'll codify fallback policies as part of the pilot runbook.
[06:19] Karen Patel: Are there any gotchas with tokenization differences? We have observed token counts differ between tokenizers.
[06:24] Liam Ortiz: Good point. We'll normalize using the tokenizer used by the model family in test. Please note token counts can vary 5-12% between families; that affects per-token cost directly. That's why we ask for raw text prompts and we'll run tokenization profiling.
[06:37] Speaker 2: (background)
[06:39] Maya Chen: Ok next, constraints for the pilot: budget cap $15k, timeline two weeks, success criteria as discussed. So we should be clear: if benchmarking shows we can't hit p95 < 350ms with cost under the cap then next steps include exploring dedicated capacity or larger commit discounts.
[06:57] Jamal Rivers: Makes sense. How will you present the final model selection?
[07:01] Liam Ortiz: We'll provide a decision matrix: model vs latency vs cost vs quality. We'll highlight operational knobs used (batch size, cache hit rates, quant level) and the recommended config for production.
[07:10] Karen Patel: Are there examples of past customers with similar scale?
[07:13] Maya Chen: Yes a retail customer with a similar qps/p95 target moved from on-prem to Redwood dedicated and saved ~35% unit cost after 3 months due to better batching and prefix caching. We can share an anonymized case study.
[07:26] Sofia Martinez: Ok. On security: we need network diagrams and KMS certification.
[07:30] Maya Chen: I'll attach SOC2, ISO summaries, and a sample network diagram. For POC we can propose a dedicated sandbox with logging retention that meets your needs.
[07:40] Jamal Rivers: About observability: how granular are token-level costs?
[07:44] Liam Ortiz: We surface per-route and per-token breakdown in the console; you can see cost by model and by route, plus trace-level latencies. That helps correlate expensive prompts to specific flows.
[07:56] Karen Patel: That will help.
[07:58] Maya Chen: Any other questions early?
[08:01] Sofia Martinez: One minor point: our infra team will want to see an example of the autoscaling policy for dedicated.
[08:06] Liam Ortiz: We'll include a recommended autoscale config with CPU/GPU thresholds, scale cooldowns, and burst policies.
[08:13] Maya Chen: Ok let's shift to the benchmark plan details — I'll read it out then we'll get commitments. Phase 1: ingest traces and prompts. Phase 2: run baseline tests 7B/13B/quant-30B. Phase 3: analyze and deliver a decision matrix and cost spreadsheet. Total 5 business days from traces receipt.
[08:32] Jamal Rivers: Agree in principle.
[08:34] Karen Patel: We can provide traces by Sunday night.
[08:37] Maya Chen: Great. We'll aim to start Monday.
[08:40] Liam Ortiz: Quick technical note: for the throughput sweep we'll vary concurrency and batch sizes and measure GPU token throughput, end-to-end latency, and p95. We'll also do a small stress test to exercise KV cache warm/cold behavior.
[08:55] Karen Patel: That cold/warm behavior is important — we have a mix of new and returning sessions.
[09:00] Maya Chen: We'll simulate a realistic user mix. Also, when we do the cost calc, we'll show three scenarios: optimistic (high cache, large batching), expected (measured traces), and conservative (low cache, small batching).
[09:14] Sofia Martinez: Is there any non-linear cost when you scale GPUs (like infra thresholds)?
[09:19] Liam Ortiz: Sometimes. For example, certain instance sizes have different performance/cost ratios; packing constraints and multi-tenant overheads can affect marginal cost. We'll capture that nuance in the model and call it out.
[09:29] Jamal Rivers: Ok last question: how will you validate quality regression after quantization?
[09:34] Liam Ortiz: We'll run your evaluation prompts and track metric diffs — exact match, Rouge, and a small human eval for edge cases. We'll flag items with >2% degradation.
[09:44] Maya Chen: Alright team, recap of next steps: Maya sends spreadsheet and compliance docs by Friday, Liam runs benchmarks starting Monday after traces, Polaris to provide traces by Sunday, follow-up scheduled for 2026-05-21 to review.
[09:58] Karen Patel: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[10:01] Sofia Martinez: Thanks.
[10:03] Jamal Rivers: Thanks.
[10:05] Maya Chen: Bye all.
[41:30] (call end)
